content: 1. Dipyrone and phenylbutazone are not recommended for use due to their associated toxicity and lack of efficacy. 2. For children with fever, ensure they are dressed lightly, kept in a warm but well-ventilated room, and encouraged to increase their oral fluid intake. 3. Pain management in children should involve the appropriate use of analgesics, tailored to the severity of the pain. 4. Administer analgesics in two steps: for mild pain and for moderate-to-severe pain. 5. Provide analgesics on a regular schedule (by the clock) to prevent the recurrence of severe pain before the next dose. 6. Use the simplest, most effective, and least painful route of administration, preferably oral. Avoid intramuscular (IM) treatment as it can be painful and delay effects in cases of shock. 7. Adjust the dose for each child individually, as children have varying dose requirements for the same effect. Titrate the dose progressively to ensure adequate pain relief. 8. For mild pain, such as headaches, post-traumatic pain, or pain due to spasticity, administer paracetamol or ibuprofen to children older than 3 months who can take oral medication. For infants younger than 3 months, use only paracetamol. 9. If morphine does not adequately relieve pain, consider switching to alternative opioids like fentanyl or hydromorphone, but monitor carefully for respiratory depression. 10. If tolerance to opioids develops, increase the dose to maintain the same level of pain relief. 11. Adjuvant medicines, such as diazepam for muscle spasm, carbamazepine for neuralgic pain, or corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) for pain due to inflammatory swelling pressing on a nerve, may be used, but evidence for their efficacy in persistent or specific pain cases in children is insufficient. 12. In cases of anemia, initiate treatment unless the child has severe acute malnutrition. Provide daily iron-folate tablets or iron syrup for 14 days and ask the parent to return with the child after 14 days. Continue treatment for 3 months if possible, as it takes 2–4 weeks to correct anemia and 1–3 months to build up iron stores. 13. For children aged 1 year or older who have not received mebendazole in the past 6 months, administer a single dose of mebendazole (500 mg) to address potential hookworm or whipworm infestation. 14. In cases of severe anemia, provide a blood transfusion as soon as possible. Use packed cells (10 mL/kg over 3–4 hours) if available, or fresh whole blood (20 mL/kg over 3–4 hours) if not. 15. Monitor respiratory and pulse rates every 15 minutes during transfusion. If either increases or there are signs of heart failure, slow the transfusion rate. 16. If fluid overload occurs due to the transfusion, administer IV furosemide at 1–2 mg/kg, up to a maximum total of 20 mg. 17. After the transfusion, reassess the child. If hemoglobin levels remain low, repeat the transfusion. 18. In children with severe acute malnutrition, fluid overload is a common and serious complication. Use packed cells or whole blood at 10 mL/kg and avoid repeating transfusions based on hemoglobin levels or within 4 days of the initial transfusion. 19. Use screened blood that is negative for transfusion-transmissible infections (e.g., malaria, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV). Do not use blood past its expiry date or blood that has been out of refrigeration for more than 2 hours. 20. Before transfusion, ensure the blood is the correct group, the patient’s name and number match the label, and the blood pack has no leaks or discoloration. 21. During transfusion, use an infusion device if available to control the rate, and monitor for signs of a transfusion reaction, especially in the first 15 minutes. 22. If a transfusion reaction occurs, stop the transfusion, remove the IV line but keep the cannula in place, and set up a new infusion with normal saline. 23. For mild hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., itchy rash), slow the transfusion and administer 1 mg/kg IM antihistamine if available. If symptoms persist, treat as a moderately severe reaction. 24. For severe reactions (e.g., fever, rigors, restlessness, raised heart rate, fast breathing, dark urine, unexplained bleeding, confusion, or collapse), stop the transfusion, maintain the airway, provide oxygen, and treat shock. Report the reaction to the doctor and blood laboratory. 25. Oxygen therapy should be guided by pulse oximetry. Administer oxygen to children with oxygen saturation below 90%. 26. Oxygen should also be given to children with very severe pneumonia, bronchiolitis, or asthma who exhibit central cyanosis, inability to drink due to respiratory distress, severe lower chest wall indrawing, respiratory rate ≥70/min, grunting with every breath, or depressed mental status. 27. Nasal prongs are the preferred method of oxygen delivery as they are safe, non-invasive, and reliable. Nasal or nasopharyngeal catheters may be used as alternatives if nasal prongs are unavailable. 28. Monitor oxygen therapy using pulse oximetry and adjust the flow rate to maintain stable oxygen saturation above 90%. 29. Continue oxygen therapy until the child can maintain oxygen saturation above 90% in room air. Gradually wean off oxygen and monitor the child’s stability. 30. For play therapy, engage children in activities that include language and motor skills, such as singing local songs, laughing, and performing motor tasks. Use simple toys like nesting toys, rattles, or dolls made from household materials to encourage development.
